patient.name: Priya Sharma
patient.complaint: Red, sticky right eye for 1 day, now spreading to the left
background: 30 weeks pregnant with her first baby
Teaching assistant in a Hounslow primary school; several children off with sticky eyes

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a red eye and discharge: watery with a cold suggests viral, purulent and stuck together suggests bacterial, bilateral itch with hay fever suggests allergic. Pain, photophobia or reduced vision means it is not simple conjunctivitis.

points: Priya woke with her **right eye glued shut**.
Gritty and sore, not truly painful.
By lunchtime the **left eye** started too.
Vision clear once she wipes the discharge away.

steps.lead: A red eye with discharge and irritation is **conjunctivitis**: inflammation of the conjunctiva. Next, decide viral, bacterial or allergic.
Priya has **infected contacts** at school, wears **contact lenses** and has **hay fever**: three risk factors.

points: Both eyes diffusely red (**conjunctival injection**), worse on the right.
Visual acuity **6/6** each eye; pupils equal and reactive.
Cornea clear; no pre-auricular node; no itch.

steps.lead: Purulent discharge and eyes stuck together in the morning point to **bacterial** conjunctivitis, not viral (watery) or allergic (itchy).

steps.q: Which feature would most strongly suggest Priya does NOT have simple conjunctivitis?
steps.r: Conjunctivitis should not cause **severe pain, photophobia or vision loss**. These suggest keratitis, uveitis or acute glaucoma.

steps.lead: Priya's vision is 6/6 and she has no photophobia or severe pain, so no **red flags**. Being a contact lens wearer, she must return if pain develops.

steps.title: Red eye: safe to call it conjunctivitis?

steps.lead: Priya's contact lenses put her at risk of **keratitis**, the key complication to watch for.
When Priya's baby arrives, purulent discharge in a **newborn** is different: think **chlamydia or gonococcus**, not simple bacterial conjunctivitis.

steps.text: **Viral** is the commonest cause overall (usually **adenovirus**). The notes call **allergic** the most common UK subtype seasonally.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where routine conjunctivitis needs none (clinical diagnosis). Swabs are for contact lens wearers, neonates, recurrent or failed cases and suspected chlamydia or gonococcus.

steps.text: Normal vision, pupils and cornea: inflammation is confined to the conjunctiva.

points: Conjunctival swab taken from the right eye.
No Acanthamoeba or Pseudomonas, the contact-lens worries.

steps.lead: If Priya's newborn develops a sticky eye, **urgent swabs** for **chlamydia and gonococcus** are needed.

steps.text: Do not swab every red eye. Swab only if **unusual, recurrent, severe**, a **contact lens wearer**, a **neonate**, or suspected gonococcal or chlamydial infection.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': no contact lenses, supportive care first, topical chloramphenicol if antibiotics are needed, topical fusidic acid in pregnancy (third trimester) or if chloramphenicol fails, and topical antihistamine for allergic conjunctivitis.

steps.lead: Priya **stops wearing her contact lenses**. Supportive care first: cold compresses, lid hygiene, her own towel, analgesia.

steps.q: Which topical antibiotic suits Priya at 31 weeks?
steps.r: **Chloramphenicol** is contraindicated in the **third trimester** (grey baby syndrome). **Fusidic acid** is safe throughout pregnancy.

steps.lead: Each spring Priya's hay fever brings itchy eyes. That is **allergic** conjunctivitis: conservative measures, then a **topical antihistamine**, and **sodium cromoglicate** if recurrent.
Priya's plan follows **NICE CKS** on infective and allergic conjunctivitis.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why viral causes watery discharge and a pre-auricular node, why bacterial is purulent, why allergic itches (type I hypersensitivity), why red flags imply deeper disease, and how chloramphenicol works.

steps.lead: Priya's **Haemophilus** infection drew in **neutrophils**, giving thick, purulent discharge.
The children at Priya's school most likely have **adenovirus**: spread by direct contact, with watery discharge and a **pre-auricular node**.

steps.title: Allergic conjunctivitis
nodes: Binds IgE on mast cells (type I)

steps.lead: Priya's spring itchy eyes are **type I, IgE-mediated** hypersensitivity: histamine causes **chemosis** and itch.
Priya's normal vision and lack of photophobia show the inflammation is **confined to the conjunctiva**, sparing the cornea and deeper eye.
Chloramphenicol is a **bacteriostatic protein synthesis inhibitor**; topical use limits systemic exposure. Priya avoided it only because of the third trimester.

steps.q: Why is a sticky eye in a 3-day-old baby treated as urgent?
o: It may be vertically transmitted gonococcus or chlamydia
steps.r: **Neisseria gonorrhoeae** and **Chlamydia trachomatis** are passed during birth and can cause serious eye and systemic disease.

steps.lead: So if Priya's baby gets purulent eyes, it is **vertically transmitted** infection until proven otherwise.

mcq.q: What is the most common overall cause of conjunctivitis?
mcq.r: **Viral**, usually adenovirus, up to 80% of cases.

mcq.q: Which discharge is classic of bacterial conjunctivitis?
mcq.r: **Purulent** discharge with crusting and eyes stuck together in the morning.

mcq.q: Which feature is typical of allergic conjunctivitis?
mcq.r: Bilateral **itch**, chemosis and **cobblestone papillae** on the tarsal conjunctiva.

mcq.q: Which symptom is a red flag in a red eye?
mcq.r: Severe pain, photophobia or vision loss suggest **keratitis, uveitis or acute glaucoma**.

mcq.q: Which patient with conjunctivitis needs a swab?
o: A child with a cold and watery eye
mcq.r: Swab if **contact lens wearer**, neonate, recurrent or failed treatment, or suspected chlamydia or gonococcus.

mcq.q: What should a contact lens wearer do during conjunctivitis?
mcq.r: **No contact lenses** at any point during the episode.

mcq.q: Why is chloramphenicol avoided in the third trimester?
mcq.r: Risk of **grey baby syndrome**; use **fusidic acid** instead.

mcq.q: What is the first-line drug for allergic conjunctivitis?
mcq.r: **Topical antihistamine** first; sodium cromoglicate for recurrent or persistent.

mcq.q: What type of hypersensitivity causes allergic conjunctivitis?
mcq.r: **Type I, IgE-mediated**: mast cell histamine release.

glossary.Conjunctiva: Thin membrane covering the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids.
glossary.Conjunctivitis: Inflammation of the conjunctiva, causing a red eye with discharge and irritation.
glossary.Conjunctival injection: Redness of the conjunctiva from dilated blood vessels.
glossary.Cobblestone papillae: Large bumps on the inner eyelid seen in allergic conjunctivitis.
glossary.Tarsal conjunctiva: Conjunctiva lining the inside of the eyelid.
glossary.Pre-auricular lymph node: Lymph node just in front of the ear; enlarged in viral conjunctivitis.
glossary.Adenovirus: DNA virus that is the commonest cause of viral conjunctivitis.
glossary.Haemophilus influenzae: Gram-negative bacterium and common cause of bacterial conjunctivitis.
glossary.Neisseria gonorrhoeae: Sexually transmitted bacterium that can infect a baby's eyes during birth.
glossary.Chlamydia trachomatis: Sexually transmitted organism that can cause neonatal conjunctivitis.
glossary.Ophthalmia neonatorum: Conjunctivitis in the first 28 days of life.
glossary.Vertical transmission: Passing an infection from mother to baby during pregnancy or birth.
glossary.Keratitis: Inflammation or infection of the cornea; sight-threatening, especially in contact lens wearers.
glossary.Uveitis: Inflammation of the uvea, causing pain, photophobia and blurred vision.
glossary.Acute angle-closure glaucoma: Sudden rise in eye pressure causing a painful red eye, haloes, vomiting and reduced vision.
glossary.Photophobia: Pain or discomfort on exposure to light.
glossary.Visual acuity: Sharpness of vision, measured on a Snellen chart (6/6 is normal).
glossary.Fluorescein: Orange dye that stains damaged corneal epithelium green under blue light.
glossary.Atopy: Inherited tendency to allergic disease such as asthma, eczema and hay fever.
glossary.Chloramphenicol: Topical broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotic; first choice for bacterial conjunctivitis.
glossary.Fusidic acid: Topical antibiotic safe throughout pregnancy; second line for bacterial conjunctivitis.
glossary.Grey baby syndrome: Circulatory collapse in neonates who cannot metabolise chloramphenicol.
glossary.Aplastic anaemia: Bone marrow failure; a rare risk with systemic chloramphenicol.
glossary.Bacteriostatic: Stops bacteria multiplying rather than killing them outright.
glossary.Sodium cromoglicate: Mast cell stabiliser eye drop for recurrent or persistent allergic conjunctivitis.
glossary.Mast cell stabiliser: Drug that prevents mast cells releasing histamine.
glossary.Type I hypersensitivity: Immediate, IgE-mediated allergic reaction with mast cell degranulation.
glossary.Rescue antibiotic: An antibiotic used only if symptoms do not improve after a set time.
glossary.URTI: Upper respiratory tract infection, such as a cold.
glossary.NICE CKS: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries, UK primary care guidance.

technique.stem: A 9 year old boy has 2 days of a red left eye that started after a cold. It now affects the right eye too. The eyes are gritty and watering with no pus. His sister had the same last week. Visual acuity is normal and there is a tender pre-auricular lymph node. His temperature is 37.4°C and pulse rate 92 bpm.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A red eye diagnosis: first rule out red flags, then type the conjunctivitis.
URTI, one eye then the other, watery, infected contact, node.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Glaucoma: older adult, severe pain, reduced vision, haloes.
Allergic: itch is dominant and both eyes start together; no node.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: watery + URTI + pre-auricular node = viral.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman has a 2 day history of a red, sticky left eye. She has thick yellow discharge and her eyelids are stuck together each morning. It is now starting in the right eye. There is no itch, pain or photophobia. Visual acuity is 6/6. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Purulent discharge with eyes stuck together in the morning is bacterial conjunctivitis. Normal vision and no pain or photophobia exclude keratitis and glaucoma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Glaucoma causes severe pain and reduced vision.

practice.stem: A 17 year old boy has had red, intensely itchy, watering eyes in both eyes for 3 weeks every May. He also sneezes and has a runny nose. He has eczema and asthma. There is conjunctival swelling and cobblestone papillae under the upper lids. There is no purulent discharge. Visual acuity is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Bilateral itchy watery eyes, seasonal, with rhinitis, atopy, chemosis and cobblestone papillae is allergic conjunctivitis. No pus argues against bacterial.

steps.x: Itch, bilateral, seasonal, atopic, classic signs, no pus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Blepharitis gives crusty lid margins, chronic and non-seasonal.
Episcleritis is a localised red patch, not itchy.
Viral is watery after a cold, not seasonal with cobblestones.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: itch + hay fever + both eyes = allergic.

practice.stem: A 7 year old girl has a red, watery right eye for 3 days that is now affecting the left eye. She had a sore throat and runny nose last week, and two classmates have red eyes. There is a palpable pre-auricular lymph node. Visual acuity is normal. Her temperature is 37.6°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Watery conjunctivitis after an URTI with a pre-auricular node and infected contacts is viral, most commonly adenovirus. Haemophilus and S. aureus cause purulent bacterial conjunctivitis.

steps.x: Organism: first decide viral or bacterial.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Chlamydia is neonatal or sexually acquired.
HSV gives vesicles and dendritic corneal ulcers, usually one eye.

practice.stem: A 3 day old baby boy has swollen eyelids and copious purulent discharge from both eyes. He was born by vaginal delivery. His mother did not attend antenatal care and her partner has recently had a urethral discharge. The baby's temperature is 37.3°C and pulse rate 150 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Purulent conjunctivitis in a neonate after vaginal delivery with a parental STI history suggests vertically transmitted Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which typically appears in the first few days of life.

steps.x: Organism in a newborn sticky eye.
Neonate, hyperpurulent, early, vertical STI risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Haemophilus is the common bacterial cause in older children and adults.
S. aureus does not explain the STI history.
S. pneumoniae does not explain the STI history.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: neonate + pus = think gonococcus or chlamydia.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman who wears monthly contact lenses was treated for conjunctivitis 4 days ago and continued wearing her lenses. She now has severe right eye pain, marked photophobia and blurred vision. Visual acuity in the right eye is 6/24. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which complication has most likely developed?
practice.e: Keratitis is the key complication of conjunctivitis in contact lens wearers: severe pain, photophobia, reduced vision and corneal fluorescein staining. It needs same-day ophthalmology review.

clues: severe right eye pain, marked photophobia
steps.x: Lens wearer with red flags and corneal staining.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Glaucoma: older, fixed mid-dilated pupil, haloes, no staining.
Uveitis does not stain the cornea and is not linked to lenses.
Orbital cellulitis gives lid swelling, fever and painful eye movements.
A painless red patch with normal vision.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: lens wearer + pain + photophobia + reduced vision = keratitis.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has a 1 day history of a red, sticky right eye with crusted lashes. He is otherwise well. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. You suspect bacterial conjunctivitis.

o: Normal visual acuity and reactive pupils

practice.e: In conjunctivitis vision and pupils are normal with no major corneal abnormality. A fixed mid-dilated pupil and corneal haze suggest acute glaucoma.

steps.x: Expected examination finding in bacterial conjunctivitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Normal vision and pupils**, conjunctival injection and discharge.
**B.** Rule: conjunctivitis spares vision, pupils and cornea.

practice.stem: A 19 year old man has intensely itchy, red, swollen conjunctivae within minutes of mowing the lawn each summer. He has hay fever and asthma. There is marked chemosis. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 76 bpm.
